question: A new pronunciation takes hold in a city over several generations. What shape does its spread usually trace?
options: Slow start, fast middle, slow finish
Steady gains, about equal each decade
answer: Slow start, fast middle, slow finish. At first few speakers meet the new form, so it creeps; once many use it, each user exposes others and the change surges; the last holdouts, often the oldest and most isolated, take longest. Plotted against time, changes in many languages trace this S-shaped curve.
move: Early slowness says little about how fast something will spread later.
trap: Picturing a change creeping forward by the same amount each decade.
reference: Blythe & Croft, S-curves and the mechanisms of propagation in language change, Language 88(2), 2012
